You and Mii.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort releases tomorrow (22nd October), and Nintendo is making sure that launch day goes smoothly by releasing its very first update.
The ver. 1.1.0 update is now available. As is often the case with these launch-day jobbies, its purpose is mainly to enable all of the online modes so everyone can play some non-local multiplayer right from the jump. That said, the update also introduces a Mii frequency adjuster, where you can choose how often your Miis appear in offline competitive sports.

Wibble-wobble.
At a glance, JSAUX’s 6-in-1 Dock for the Switch 2 is a compelling piece of kit.
In addition to docking your console for TV mode, it also contains four slots to charge Joy-Con, along with space to charge your Pro Controller. With a foldable design, it makes for a handy travel companion, and the slick display screen is a neat little touch that will no doubt draw a few eyes. There are, however, a few glaring issues that hold it back.

The store (not referred to as a 'Pokémon Center' in TPC's official statement, interestingly) will open by 2029, and will offer "a variety of exclusive merchandise and one-of-a-kind experiences for Trainers of all ages".

articles.description:
Eye spy.
Creepy space horror Mouthwashing became something of an indie sensation when it launched back in 2024. After racking up over 500,000 Steam sales, publisher Critical Reflex announced that a Switch version was in the works and now (a year on from that announcement), we finally have a release date.
As revealed in yesterday's Xbox Showcase, Mouthwashing will launch on the Switch eShop on 29th October — yep, as in next week. It's already available to pre-order on the North American storefront, in fact, for $12.99. We've noticed that the store lists its release date as 10th October, but we're sure that's just a typo (we've reached out to Critical Reflex just to double-check). 
Read the full article on nintendolife.com

articles.description:
Good to have you back, old friend.
Over the years, Final Fantasy has been nothing if not inventive, as its largely anthology-based approach has led to a variety of JRPG game design experiments. Yet in more recent years, it feels like the franchise has strayed from its roots, with more old-school fans pining for a return to the days when Final Fantasy was focused on being an RPG first and foremost.
Such fans can rejoice, as that mythical return has finally arrived in the form of Final Fantasy Resonance. Though much noise has been made about this being a retooled version of the decommissioned mobile gacha game Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, this is a massive oversimplification of what Square did with this project. While it may be based upon the plot of that mobile entry, this is a completely new, true-blue classic Final Fantasy that celebrates the series' legacy. If you enjoyed any of the older turn-based Final Fantasy games, this is the game you've been waiting for.
Read the full article on nintendolife.com
articles.title: Review: Final Fantasy Resonance (Switch 2) - Plays Like A Lost Entry From Earlier In The Series

Perhaps slightly less like everyone else, I also took things far too seriously in the forgotten Wii Sports Club on Wii U, and Nintendo Switch Sports stands as one of my most-played games on the titular hardware.

articles.description:
This time it's war.
What is a Castlevania game? Nothing but a miserable little melting pot of horror tropes drawn from famous literary archetypes—Carpathian gothica populated by Universal monsters and their lesser minions—with inspirations that run the gamut from Scandinavian folklore to Greek myth. Schematically, it is a series of platform-navigation sequences interspersed with combat encounters, levelling, magic, and weapon forging across a Metroid-inspired map.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is all of these things, and is therefore acceptable as part of the series’ evolution. Its basic tenet is live, die, repeat: becoming incrementally stronger until everything crumbles before your might. The rub, as it were, is that it so closely resembles a thousand other games that it needs to scream to be heard.
Read the full article on nintendolife.com
articles.title: Review: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse (Switch) - A Pro-Grade Metroidvania With A Stiff Learning Curve

articles.author: Julian Benson
articles.description:
You know when you follow someone into the elevator and when they turn around to face the doors, you choose to stand still and instead meet their eyes? No, of course you don't. Everyone knows that when you're in a lift you don't under any circumstances face other people in the lift unless you know them and you're already in a conversation. Just yesterday I got into the lift with someone I sit one desk over from in the office. I dutifully looked at my phone the entire time until we were safely out of the building. Well, in the puzzle game How To Ride Elevators Like A Human you play a helpful alien who saves people who have accidentally ended up in the dreadful situation of facing one another.
Each short puzzle takes place in a compact lift where one (or several) humans are starting at each other. Using your small UFO's tractor beam, you must pick up and relocate the passengers until no one is making eyes at anyone else. You may well recognise this as a sokoban-style puzzle game, but, despite retreading familiar ground, I'm a big fan of this extraterrestrial framing. Even if I have an ulterior motive for sharing this game...
Read more
articles.title: A puzzle game where you must avoid the doing the most awkward of things: facing someone while riding an elevator

articles.author: James Archer
articles.description:
One of the most memorable demos I played at Gamescom Latam 2026 was that of Talaka, a watercoloured 2D action-roguelike that - like many games at the São Paulo-based show – leaned deeply into Brazilian culture and mythology. In this case, it's something of a side-scrolling Hades, with the permahorny Greek gods replaced by a playful pantheon of Orishas (vaguely human-shaped forces of nature) hailing from the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religion. Though no fault of theirs, I kinda sucked at Talaka when I played it then, and the demo currently available during Steam Next Fest confirms I kinda suck at it now – though it's still colourful enough, and steeped in a folklore that games so rarely explore, that I'm going to keep an eye on it.
Read more
articles.title: I keep embarrassing myself in front of the nature gods in handpainted 2D roguelike Talaka, whose colourful, combative demo is out now

articles.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
articles.description:
Prominent capital-p Political game developer and left-wing academic Paulo "Molleindustria" Pedercini has revealed that he used generative AI tools for aspects of recent ecosocialist satire Future? No Thanks!. According to Pedercini, "a tiny fraction of its code was written with AI support" towards the end of the project, specifically to assess and fix bugs.
The game also uses text-to-speech voice-acting for a couple of characters, generated with ElevenLab software, with Pedercini noting that the characters in question are intended as a spoof of wonky artificial intelligence. He insists that none of the game's art or writing is AI-generated. These insights arrive weeks after the game's Steam release, which was delayed due to Valve's concerns about sexual material. Back then, there was no genAI disclosure on the game's storepage. There is one now.
 Read more
articles.title: "AI is a technofascist, anti-human and anti-art project", says creator of lefty tech satire Future? No Thanks!, before explaining why he used it anyway

articles.description:
Bracingly moist open world survival game Subnautica 2 is embarking on the "voyage to early access 2.0" - this being developer Unknown Worlds' excitable term for the next round of updates, which will include a new region, creature, and Tadpole chassis, plus some tweaks for biomods and creature behaviour.
I like Subnautica 2 and am happy that Unknown Worlds appear to be enjoying some stability, after all the firings and ChatGPT-abetted lawyer-wrestling over publisher earn-outs, but I really hate "early access 2.0". I know other teams use nomenclature like this, but seriously, what even is time any more? You can't make a sequel to something you haven't finished! It's 8.30 in the morning, Unknown Worlds, and I already have a migraine. Let's hurry on to the talk of spooky new regions.

Incremental games often have that effect, and Selkie's Salvage&Co. is no different in that regard, it's just the funny thing is that it is essentially a game about taking your rubbish out.

articles.description:
Earlier this year, I embarked on a pivotal journey, one that I'm sure upon finishing will change me for good: I started watching Haikyu!! It's my first sports anime (when you're a chubby little muffin like I was, you take more interest in Not Moving over Sports), an abscess in the lexicon of genres I've dipped my toes into, one I'm rectifying after all these years. And friends, it's good eatin'. I even, incredibly briefly, floated the idea of taking up volleyball. Yet now I don't have to, and it's all thanks to a delightful, incredibly Wii Sports coded game called just volleyball.

It's a lot, of course, but it's got some lush pixel art and a demo you can try out for yourself as part of this Steam Next Fest, too.

Despite being a lover of the King of the Monsters, I was unfortunately too young to experience Pipeworks Software's Godzilla trilogy of 3D kaiju-fighters back its PS2/Gamecube-era heyday (there was a PS2 in the house as a young child, but I also had no agency to ask for games or money to buy them). As such, I'm not necessarily the intended audience for Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered, a remake of Pipeworks' first entry back in 2002, but I can gladly tell you thanks to my time with the Steam Next Fest demo that nostalgia is not needed to enjoy this classic made anew.
